source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training
finding: Three meta-analyses (chess, music, WM training) on children's cognitive and academic skills. Effects are small to moderate and shrink as design quality rises, for example with active controls.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref). No study-level numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Full text blocked (HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: Skill gained in one domain should not be assumed to lift others. Test any scaffold gain on held-out domains against an active control.
quote: far transfer of learning rarely occurs

source: Sala & Gobet (2016) Do the benefits of chess instruction transfer to academic and cognitive skills? (as summarised in Frontiers 2017 review)
finding: Chess instruction showed modest transfer in a meta-analysis, but almost no included study used an active control.
numbers: 24 studies, 40 effect sizes. Mean d: maths 0.38, overall cognitive ability 0.34, literacy 0.25. More hours gave larger effects (25-30 h suggested minimum).
limits: Passive controls cannot rule out motivation or placebo effects. Second-hand summary of the meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Headline gains from a trained skill may be placebo-like. Compare against a matched-effort control prompt, not only a no-scaffold baseline.
quote: almost none of the reviewed studies compared chess-treated groups with active control groups

source: Jerrim et al. (2016) Institute of Education randomised trial of chess in schools (as reported in Frontiers 2017 review)
finding: Large randomised trial of chess lessons found no effect on any outcome.
numbers: Year 5 pupils: 1,965 in chess, 1,900 in passive control, randomised by class. 25-30 h of chess. Post-test one year later. No outcome differed.
limits: Delayed post-test and ceiling effect (maths mean 70%, SD 20%) limit sensitivity, as the review authors note.
agent_relevance: A large randomised null outweighs many small positives. Weight our own evidence the same way.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Does chess instruction improve mathematical problem-solving ability? Two experimental studies with an active control group
finding: Title seen in a PubMed listing only. The abstract page needed cookies and was not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: None yet.

source: Sala, Aksayli, Tatlidil, Gondo, Gobet (2019) Near and far transfer in cognitive training: a second-order meta-analysis (Collabra)
finding: Meta-analysis of meta-analyses. WM training gives near transfer. Far transfer is small or null across WM training, video games, music, chess and exergames. With placebo and publication bias controlled, the overall effect and true variance were zero.
numbers: Model 1 (near transfer) k = 99. Model 2 k = 119. Model 3 k = 233 (adds six meta-analyses of video games, music, chess, exergames).
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref). 'Invariant of human cognition' is a strong claim; bias corrections are disputed by training proponents.
agent_relevance: Strongest summary warning for the project: expect gains on near tasks only.
quote: The lack of generalization of skills acquired by training is thus an invariant of human cognition.

source: Sala, Tatlidil, Gobet (2018) Video game training does not enhance cognitive ability: a comprehensive meta-analytic investigation (Psychological Bulletin)
finding: Video game skill is only weakly related to cognitive ability, and training shows no causal far-transfer effect.
numbers: Three random-effects models: skill-cognition correlation k = 310; players vs non-players k = 315; training studies k = 359. Overall effects small or null.
limits: Abstract only (via Europe PMC). Does not rule out transfer from action games to specific perceptual tasks.
agent_relevance: Matches the subfield note that video game to attention transfer is often absent.
quote: Video game training thus represents no exception to the general difficulty of obtaining far transfer.

source: Unsworth, Redick, McMillan, Hambrick, Kane, Engle (2015) Is playing video games related to cognitive abilities? Psychological Science
finding: Extreme-groups comparison made gamers look better. Across the full range of players and at the latent-variable level, nearly all relations were near zero.
numbers: Two experiments with WM, fluid intelligence and attention-control measures. Exact N not read.
limits: Abstract only. A 2017 critique argued some games, but not others, relate to ability.
agent_relevance: Extreme-group designs inflate effects. Use full-range analyses when comparing arms.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: WM training improves trained and intermediate measures but not far-transfer measures against treated controls. WM gain did not predict far-transfer size. No evidential value remained after publication-bias analysis.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 experimental comparisons.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Training the 'engine' (WM) did not help downstream skills; analogous to strengthening one reasoning module and expecting broad gains.

source: Simons et al. (2016) Do 'brain-training' programs work? (Psychological Science in the Public Interest)
finding: Review of all studies cited by brain-training companies against best-practice standards. Two open letters disagreed on the evidence.
numbers: Letters signed by 70+ scientists (sceptical) and 133 scientists (supportive). Per-study results not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Borrow the standards: active control, preregistration, outcomes on untrained real tasks.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education and professions: a meta-analysis (PubMed abstract)
finding: Deliberate practice explains much in games, music and sports, little in education, almost nothing in professions.
numbers: Variance explained (abstract): games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions under 1%. A 2018 corrigendum exists; the 2020 review cites games 24, music 23, sports 20, education 5, professions 1, overall 14%, from 88 studies.
limits: Two sets of figures exist. Cite the corrected ones with care.
agent_relevance: Practice amount predicts skill best in stable, rule-bound domains. Open-ended reasoning is nearer the weak end.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020) Is the deliberate practice view defensible? (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Deliberate practice matters but is not sufficient. Corrected variance claims depend heavily on assumed reliability.
numbers: Macnamara 2014: k = 157, r = .38, 14.4% uncorrected. Platz 2014 music: r = .61, 37.2%. Sports (Macnamara 2016): r = .45, 20.3%; elite athletes only, about 1%. Miller 2019: r = .40, 16%. Ericsson & Harwell 2019: r = .56 (8 effects). Corrected variance for the same data runs from 87.1% to 38.7% depending on assumed reliability 0.60 to 0.90.
limits: Authors belong to one side of the dispute; Ericsson's camp disagrees. Reliability assumptions cannot be verified.
agent_relevance: Same data, wide answers. Report our own effect sizes with sensitivity ranges.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020) review: individual differences and early specialisation
finding: Ability and genes still matter at high skill, and early specialisation does not predict elite status.
numbers: Gullich 2017: 83 international medalists vs 83 non-medalists; medalists had about 948 fewer organised training hours by age 18 and started about 1.5 years later. Intelligence explained about 30% of piano learning-rate differences (Burgoyne 2019). Circumvention-of-limits hypothesis supported by only 3 of 15 studies.
limits: Secondary summary of other work, not re-checked.
agent_relevance: More tuning does not remove base-capacity limits; a stronger base model may matter more than more scaffold.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Facing facts about deliberate practice (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Deliberate practice accounts for about a third of reliable variance in chess and music, so other factors are needed.
numbers: About one third of reliable variance per domain. Platz music r = .61 across 13 studies. Jabusch 2009: lifetime practice predicted only 17% of pianists' baseline variance.
limits: Argument piece, little new data.
agent_relevance: Practice-based accounts leave most variance unexplained.
quote: not as important as Ericsson and colleagues have argued

source: Macnamara & Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Romer (1993), Royal Society Open Science
finding: Preregistered double-blind replication of the classic violinist study failed to reproduce complete correspondence between skill level and practice alone.
numbers: Replication N = 39 (13 best, 13 good, 13 less accomplished) vs original N = 30 (10 per group). Effect substantial but considerably smaller than original. Teacher-designed practice did not explain more variance than practice alone. Best violinists began at 5.46 years (95% CI 3.93-6.99).
limits: Small samples, one conservatory, retrospective self-reported practice, younger sample (mean 20.8 vs 23.1).
agent_relevance: The 'practice explains everything' claim behind many training programmes is weaker than assumed.
quote: We did not replicate the core finding

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2017) The holistic processing account of visual expertise in medical image perception: a review (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Experts' eye movements show holistic processing in their own domain, but the skill is narrow and does not carry to control tasks or neighbouring modalities.
numbers: Radiologists detected 70% of abnormalities at 200 ms (Kundel & Nodine 1975). Mammography: experts found 71% of lesions in 25 s, novices 46% in 40 s. Experts use foveal vision on about 15-20% of the image. Radiologists did not beat novices on WALDO or NINA searches or on non-medical image memory. Chest-film expertise did not transfer to mammography.
limits: Many studies have small expert samples. Some timing differences were non-significant (Donovon & Litchfield 2013). A 250 ms preview did not improve accuracy (Litchfield & Donovan 2016).
agent_relevance: Perceptual expertise is domain-bound. A skill learned on one task type may not show up on another.

source: Reingold, Charness, Pomplun, Stampe (2001) Visual span in expert chess players (as reported in Sheridan & Reingold 2017)
finding: Chess experts have a larger visual span than weaker players, but only for meaningful positions, not random ones.
numbers: No numbers given in the review.
limits: Second-hand. Original paper not read.
agent_relevance: The expert advantage depends on recognisable structure; random or novel structure removes it.

source: Campitelli, Connors, Bilalic, Hambrick (2015) Psychological perspectives on expertise (editorial, Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Editorial of a 35-article collection in five themes. Video-game expertise showed no transfer to selective attention or working memory. Eye-tracking papers show experts separate relevant from irrelevant regions fast.
numbers: 35 articles. Chess study of 1,383 players over 10 years: exponential learning curves fit better than power functions. Music deliberate-practice meta-analysis r_c = .61. Chess education review found significant academic effects.
limits: Editorial summary; underlying papers not read.
agent_relevance: Maps the programme. Its transfer papers confirm narrow transfer; its eye-tracking papers suggest pruning irrelevant input first.

source: Asymmetry of working memory training transfer: systematic review and meta-analysis (2026, PMC13553679)
finding: Recent meta-analysis finds near transfer within WM is small and direction-dependent. Far transfer is essentially zero for span training.
numbers: 55 studies, 208 effect sizes, N = 3,492. Within-WM g = 0.146. Updating to span g = 0.176 (42 studies). Span to updating g = 0.048, n.s. (16 studies). Updating to non-WM g = 0.120 (35 studies). Span to non-WM g = 0.008, n.s. (11 studies). Asymmetry larger at doses of 5 h or less and in children.
limits: Direction difference only marginal (p = .073 and .076). Analyses added at revision; not preregistered. Authors not identified from the page.
agent_relevance: Even near transfer is asymmetric: training A can help B without B helping A.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does math reasoning improve general LLM capabilities? Understanding transferability of LLM reasoning
finding: Over 20 reasoning-tuned models tested. Most that excel at math fail to carry gains elsewhere. Supervised fine-tuning on math damaged general skills; RL on math transferred.
numbers: Qwen3-14B, 47K math problems. Non-reasoning average: base 45.7, SFT(think) 21.1, SFT(no-think) 29.0, RL 53.2. Other reasoning: base 30.2, SFT 45.3, RL 60.0. Math: base 27.7, SFT 49.8, RL 53.8. Transfer index to non-reasoning: SFT think -104.1, RL +52.2.
limits: One model family for the controlled study. Transfer index is the authors' own definition.
agent_relevance: Training method decides transfer. For a scaffold with no training, check gains on unrelated tasks.
quote: most models that succeed in math fail to transfer their gains to other domains

source: Huan et al. (2025) latent-shift analysis
finding: RL changes internal representations and token choices least. SFT shifts them most, matching the forgetting.
numbers: PCA shift on non-reasoning tasks: Qwen3-14B no-think 129.8, SFT no-think 113.7, SFT think 38.2, RL 36.9. KL on MATH-500: SFT no-think 0.372 vs RL 0.084. Qwen3-8B ablation: off-policy SFT TI_non -40.5, on-policy RL +32.4.
limits: Small-scale ablation on 8B and 14B models.
agent_relevance: Small on-policy changes preserve general skill. Prefer light scaffolding over heavy rewriting of behaviour.

source: Xie et al. (2025) Play to generalize: learning to reason through game play (ViGaL)
finding: RL on the video game Snake (and rotation puzzles) improved a 7B vision-language model on math and spatial benchmarks. A direct AI test of 'video games to cognition'.
numbers: Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Math avg 47.7 base, 49.4 Snake, 50.6 Snake+Rotation. MathVista 68.0 to 70.7. CLEVR+ avg 54.9 to 82.6. MMMU val 54.3 to 55.8. VSI-Bench 36.7 to 38.7. General visual 72.4 vs 72.2. Ablation (base 49.1): RL 62.3, SFT 47.2, random rewards 49.4.
limits: Single model; no variance reported. Text and tables disagree (59.5 to 61.4 vs 62.3; 63.1 vs 64.7). Math gains are a few points.
agent_relevance: Method (RL, real rewards) drove transfer; SFT and random rewards did not. Consistent with Huan.

source: Xie et al. (2025) ViGaL: comparison with direct math training
finding: A game-trained model nearly matched a model trained directly on math data.
numbers: MM-Eureka-Qwen-7B (math RL) math avg 50.1 vs ViGaL Snake+Rotation 50.6. Adding MMK12 math data raised it to 51.8.
limits: Benchmarks share spatial structure with the games, so transfer may be near rather than far.
agent_relevance: Transfer is stronger where structure is shared with the training task.

source: Xie et al. (2025) Logic-RL: unleashing LLM reasoning with rule-based reinforcement learning
finding: Training on synthetic Knights and Knaves puzzles transferred to competition maths.
numbers: Under 5,000 puzzles, 3,600 steps, 7B model. K&K average 0.19 to 0.89. 8-person puzzles (out of distribution) +0.48. AIME +125% and AMC +38% relative. DeepSeek-R1 averages 0.81; o3-mini-high 0.94.
limits: Relative gains from a low base; absolute scores only in a figure. No variance or run count reported. Authors say large-scale real maths untested.
agent_relevance: A far-looking transfer result, but from a low base and unreplicated here.
quote: improves by 125% on AIME and 38% on AMC

source: Chu et al. (2025) SFT memorizes, RL generalizes
finding: On out-of-distribution variants RL transfers and SFT breaks.
numbers: Llama-3.2-Vision-11B. Rule shift GP-L: RL 11.5 to 15.0, SFT 11.5 to 3.4. V-IRL-L: RL 80.8 to 91.8, SFT 80.8 to 1.3. Visual shift V-IRL-VL: RL 16.7 to 77.8, SFT 16.7 to 11.1 (mini benchmark best 77.8 vs 44.0 before).
limits: Two tasks, one base model. Variants stay close to the training distribution.
agent_relevance: Transfer needs shared structure plus outcome-based training.

source: Aryabumi et al. (2024) To code, or not to code? Exploring impact of code in pre-training
finding: Adding code to pre-training improves natural-language reasoning and other skills, not only code.
numbers: Models 470M to 2.8B. Up to +8.2% relative NL reasoning, +4.2% world knowledge, +6.6% generative win-rate, 12x code performance.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A positive far-transfer signal in LLMs, but it comes from pre-training, not prompting.

source: Betley et al. (2025) Emergent misalignment: narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
finding: Training on a narrow task (writing insecure code) shifted behaviour broadly. Transfer can be unwanted.
numbers: 6,000 insecure-code examples vs 6,000 secure control. GPT-4o insecure: 19.8% misaligned (+-7.1) on main questions; secure and educational-insecure controls about 0%. Backdoor model under 0.1% without trigger, about 50% with it. Open models weaker; highest Mistral-Small 7.3%.
limits: Strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. Cause not established.
agent_relevance: Narrow changes can spread; check effects outside the target domain.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Grandmaster-level chess without search
finding: A 270M transformer trained on 10M games with Stockfish labels reached grandmaster-level play with no search: expert skill from data alone in one domain.
numbers: 270M: tournament Elo 2299, Lichess blitz vs humans 2895 (174 games), vs bots 2299 (228 games), puzzles 95.4%. 9M model puzzles 88.9%, 136M 94.5%. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: bots Elo 1755, puzzles 66.5%.
limits: No transfer analysis. Paper lists limits (repetition, indecision when winning, not tournament-speed).
agent_relevance: Expert skill is domain-bound; nothing here shows it moving to other tasks.
